facts.text: Before mitosis begins, during interphase, the cell copies its DNA, so each chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere. Human body cells have 46 chromosomes. Mitosis then produces two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell and to each other, each with 46 chromosomes. Mitosis is how the body grows and repairs itself: when you scrape your knee, skin cells around the scrape divide by mitosis to make new cells that fill the gap. Mitosis works like sharing a recipe book between two kitchens: every page is photocopied and each page stays clipped to its copy; then the clips come undone and each kitchen gets one complete, identical book. The pages match chromosomes, a page clipped to its copy matches two sister chromatids, the clip matches the point where they join, and the two kitchens match the two daughter cells.

Mitosis has four stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. In prophase, the first stage, the chromosomes coil up tightly into visible X shapes and the nuclear envelope breaks down, which lets the spindle fibers reach the chromosomes; spindle fibers grow out from the two opposite poles of the cell. In metaphase, spindle fibers from both poles attach to each chromosome at its centromere, and the chromosomes line up single file across the middle of the cell. This lineup puts one sister chromatid of every chromosome facing each pole, so each side will get one copy of every chromosome.

In anaphase, the spindle fibers shorten and pull the sister chromatids of each chromosome apart, toward opposite poles; once separated, each chromatid counts as its own chromosome, so each pole ends up with one full set, 46 in a human body cell. In telophase, a nuclear envelope forms around each set and the chromosomes loosen up again. Then in cytokinesis the cytoplasm divides: in an animal cell a cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two, while a plant cell builds a cell plate. The result is two identical daughter cells.

A common mistake is to think the chromosomes are copied during mitosis; in fact the DNA is copied before mitosis, during interphase, and mitosis only separates copies that already exist. If one pair of sister chromatids fails to separate in anaphase, an error called nondisjunction, both chromatids are pulled to the same pole, so in a human body cell one daughter cell gets 47 chromosomes and the other gets 45. Cells with the wrong number of chromosomes often fail to work properly or die. Mitosis makes identical body cells; the next topic, meiosis, makes sex cells with half the number of chromosomes.

lesson_markdown:
## How does one cell split into two identical cells?

When you scrape your knee, skin cells around the scrape divide by mitosis to make new cells that fill the gap. Each new cell gets the same 46 chromosomes as the cell it came from. The big idea: **the cell copies every chromosome first, then mitosis pulls the copies apart evenly, so both new cells match.**

Picture sharing a recipe book between two kitchens. Each page is a chromosome. Every page is photocopied, and each page stays clipped to its copy, just as two sister chromatids stay joined at the centromere. Then the clips come undone, and each kitchen, a daughter cell, gets one complete, identical book.

### Step by step

1. **Copy every page (interphase).** Before mitosis begins, the cell copies its DNA, so each chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere.

   A common mistake is to think mitosis copies the chromosomes. In fact the DNA is copied before mitosis, during interphase, and mitosis only separates copies that already exist.

2. **Clear the way (prophase).** The chromosomes coil up tightly into visible X shapes, and the nuclear envelope breaks down. With the envelope gone, spindle fibers growing out from the two opposite poles of the cell can reach the chromosomes.

3. **Line up the pairs (metaphase).** Spindle fibers from both poles attach to each chromosome at its centromere, and the chromosomes line up single file across the middle of the cell. This lineup puts one sister chromatid of every chromosome facing each pole.

4. **Anaphase.** What do you think happens when the spindle fibers shorten? They pull the sister chromatids of each chromosome apart, toward opposite poles: the clips come undone. Once separated, each chromatid counts as its own chromosome, so each pole ends up with one full set, 46 in a human body cell.

5. **Two kitchens, two books (telophase and cytokinesis).** In telophase, a nuclear envelope forms around each set and the chromosomes loosen up again. Then in cytokinesis the cytoplasm divides: in an animal cell a cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two, while a plant cell builds a cell plate. The result is two identical daughter cells.

### When a pair won't separate

If one pair of sister chromatids fails to separate in anaphase, an error called nondisjunction, both chromatids are pulled to the same pole. In a human body cell, one daughter cell then gets 47 chromosomes and the other gets 45. Cells with the wrong number of chromosomes often fail to work properly or die.

Next in the course comes meiosis, which makes sex cells with half the number of chromosomes.

**Check yourself:** Mitosis itself copies nothing, so why do both daughter cells still end up with a full, identical set of chromosomes?

Want to dig into any step? Ask a follow-up question.

Interphase: DNA copied → two sister chromatids per chromosome
Prophase: envelope breaks down → spindle fibers reach chromosomes
Metaphase: chromosomes line up mid-cell → one chromatid faces each pole
